AWARD  Vide this award, the Tribunal shall decide the MACT claim petition bearing no. 41/20 under section 166(4) & 140 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 filed for the petitioners against the respondents as mentioned in the memo of parties.
FACTS OF THE CASE 1.
Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that on 14.10.2019, at about 10:30 pm, one Wasim (since deceased) was waiting for transport at Mahamaya Flyover.

It has been alleged that a Canter bearing registration no. UP-13AT-0172 was being driven rashly and negligently by its driver i.e. the R1 herein this case, and it hit the aforesaid Wasim due to which the latter sustained injuries.
It has been further alleged that the said Waseem was thereupon rushed to J.P. hospital, where he expired during his treatment on 15.10.2019 itself.

His postmortem was conducted at mortuary of Janpad,
Distt. Gautam Buddh Nagar, U.P.
A FIR in this regard was also registered MACT No. 41/20 Gulshan & Ors. Vs. Rinku Singh & Ors.

sentences.text: However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. Vs Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs Amir Chand & Ors, 2011 (1) SCR 1906 (Civil Appeal No. 1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co.
ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.

24. Having ruled so, this Tribunal now proceeds to assess the wrongful act, neglect or default of R-1,
if any, in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
Admittedly, R-1 has not explained the circumstances under which his vehicle (i.e. the offending Canter) hit the deceased Waseem.

In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the deceased or any other such person, the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.

sentences.text: The right to consortium would include the company, care, help, comfort, guidance, solace and affection of the deceased, which is a loss to his entire family.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of MACT No. 41/20 Gulshan &
Ors. Vs. Rinku Singh & Ors. Page No. 7 of 20 rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. Vs Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs Amir Chand & Ors, 2011 (1) SCR 1906 (Civil Appeal No. 1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co.
ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
19.
Both the said witnesses have categorically stated in their examination on oath that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent act of Respondent no. 1 being driver of the offending vehicle while the R2 being owner of the offending MACT No. 41/20 Gulshan & Ors. Vs. Rinku Singh & Ors.
20. Respondent no.1 i.e. driver of the offending vehicle, respondent no.2 i.e. the owner of offending vehicle and respondent no. 3 i.e. Insurance Company, have neither impeached the testimony of PW-1 & PW-2 nor in the defence evidence they have able to substantiate their claim that the accident was caused due to fault of the deceased or that they have been falsely implicated in the present case.
The evidence of the star witness in this case i.e. PW-2 on the aspect of rash and Gulshan And Ors vs Rinku Singh And Ors on 12 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/8826839/
5 negligent act of respondent no.1 while driving the offending vehicle, has remained unimpeached and his testimony has to be accepted on its face value itself as the same has successfully stood the test of cross-examination.
MACT No. 41/20 Gulshan & Ors. Vs. Rinku Singh & Ors.
In view of the above, it could be safely assumed that the offending vehicle was being driven by R-1 indeed at the time of incident and the fatal injuries to the deceased took place on account of the incident in question itself.
Admittedly, R-1 has not explained the circumstances under which his vehicle (i.e. the offending Canter) hit the deceased Waseem.
In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the deceased or any other such person, the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
In view of the above discussion, this tribunal is constrained to hold R-1 guilty of gross neglect and default in driving the offending vehicle at MACT No. 41/20 Gulshan & Ors. Vs. Rinku Singh & Ors. Page No.
10 of 20 the relevant time leading to the fatal injuries to the deceased Waseem.
25.
Furthermore, in view of the medical records, postmortem report placed on record by the petitioners, no doubt or dispute is left regarding the fatal injuries to the deceased Waseem in the above accident.
On the basis of findings upon issue no. (i), it is clear that the incident in question had occurred due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle by R-1 and fatal injuries had been caused to the deceased in the incident.
Hence, petitioners being the LRs of the deceased and being his dependents are entitled to compensation in this case.
The respondent no. 1 Rinku Singh is the principal tort feasor being driver and owner of the offending vehicle.
At the same time, the respondents have failed to bring on record or to prove any breach of the terms or conditions of the said insurance policy by the respondents no. 1 and 2 in any manner.
31. Hence, on the basis of entire above stated facts and circumstances and discussion of evidence,
this Tribunal is of the opinion that respondent no.3 i.e. insurance company is liable to pay the entire compensation to the petitioner on behalf of respondent no.1 and 2, without any recovery rights.
In the present case, perusal of the Aadhar card of Waseem Ex. PW1/3 reveal that date of birth of the deceased was 09.08.1991 and the same has not been disputed in any manner by the respondents.
Therefore, the deceased was thus aged about 28 years at the time of the incident resulting in his death on 15.10.2019.
